⚡🇺🇸🇬🇧 During the Atlantic Thunder 2026 exercise, held last month and including a ship‑sinking simulation (SINKEX) organized by the U.S. 6th Fleet, U.S. and British forces sank the decommissioned frigate Klakring (FFG 42) in the North Atlantic.
Weapons used:
SM-6 missiles from the destroyer USS Paul Ignatius (DDG-117)
Naval Strike Missile (NSM) missiles from the frigate Portland (F79)
Sea Venom missiles (Royal Navy)
Mk 48 torpedoes from the submarine Massachusetts (SSN-798)
The exercise also involved P-8 aircraft of the U.S. Navy and the Royal Air Force, as well as F-15E fighters of the U.S. Air Force.
The frigate Klakring belonged to the Oliver Hazard Perry class and served in the U.S. Navy from 1983 to 2013. It was named after Rear Admiral Thomas Klakring, a three‑time recipient of the Navy Cross who commanded the submarine Guardfish during World War II.
These drills were also the first time the Royal Navy used its new NSM and Sea Venom anti‑ship missiles against a real target.

🇮🇷 Viral USMC graphic shows what a potential amphibious assault on Iran might look like
 
USMC officer Travis Hord recently posted a report on Linkedin showing what a USMC fight for a hostile coastline might entail, highlighting 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit training modeled on an “Advance Base Operations” concept developed in 2019 “to support distributed operations in contested waters.”
The post included a graphic featuring a fictionalized map, and depicting movement of small, low-visibility USMC assets over the course of an island-hopping campaign, engagement with enemy forces, setting up forward arming and refueling points (FARPs), airfields, air defenses, scouting ops, anti-ship cruise missile fires and maritime interdiction.
The graphic also simulated the kinds of enemy surface, undersea and air attacks US forces may run up against.
Picked up by analysts including US Navy Reserve intel officer Blake Herzinger, the graphic spread virally as a “leaked Pentagon graphic” on how Marines might try to seize [Iranian islands](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71837) in amphibious assault ops.
But casual observers immediately poked holes in the plans, pointing to the immense concentration of drone and missile fire Iran would amass to fend off such assaults,[ the issues the US would face](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/67165) even trying to slip an amphibious assault group into the region, logistical issues, and the wisdom of trying to move troops even closer to Iran after the IRGC wiped out nearly all of the US’s bases in the Gulf in the first weeks of the war.

events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🇺🇸💻🇮🇷 Iran Puts America’s Gulf AI Boom on Notice
Amazon, Microsoft and Google are pouring billions into Persian Gulf data centers. Iran has warned that another US attack could put those investments, along with the undersea cables connecting them, in the line of fire.
On October 10, Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei said US-linked data centers, AI facilities and communications infrastructure across the region could become targets if America attacks Iran again.
He estimated the value of these assets at more than $2T. Rezaei stressed that Iran had not yet designated them as targets.
The warning comes as American tech giants invest heavily in turning the Gulf into a global computing hub.
Microsoft has committed $15.2B to the UAE through 2029, expanding its cloud and AI infrastructure alongside local partners. Google Cloud and Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund have announced a $10B AI hub, while Amazon is investing more than $5.3B in a Saudi cloud region.
And plenty of infrastructure is already operating.
Amazon Web Services runs cloud regions in the UAE and Bahrain. Microsoft has facilities in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Qatar, while Google and Oracle operate across Saudi Arabia and other Gulf markets.
The danger is hardly theoretical.
During the earlier US-Iran war in March, drone strikes damaged two AWS facilities in the UAE and affected another in Bahrain. Amazon confirmed structural damage, power failures and service outages that disrupted businesses and financial institutions.
Recovery proved difficult. Physical damage to cloud infrastructure can take far longer to repair than an ordinary software outage.
The region's digital connections are also exposed at sea.
Undersea fiber-optic cables running through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz connect regional networks to international communications systems. A major disruption could affect cloud access, banking services and data traffic far beyond the damaged infrastructure itself.
That makes the economic stakes considerably wider than the balance sheets of American technology companies.
Gulf governments are investing heavily in AI and cloud computing to diversify their economies. Local companies provide land, electricity and infrastructure, while US firms supply computing hardware, software and cloud platforms.
Those partnerships also tie American commercial interests more closely to the security of the countries hosting them.
Rezaei's warning expands Iran's deterrence message beyond military bases and oil facilities. American technology investments, he argues, could also become vulnerable if the US launches another attack.
For Gulf governments betting billions on becoming global AI hubs, the March AWS outages have already demonstrated how quickly a regional war can interrupt the digital services their economies increasingly depend on.

events.text:
🇾🇪🇸🇦 'Davos in the desert' called off as Houthi attacks hit Saudi airports
Saudi Arabia has called off its flagship Future Investment Initiative, the annual gathering known as "Davos in the desert," following a wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, Financial Times reports.
The event, which was due to start next week, will now take place next year. Organizers had reportedly considered holding the event virtually on the original dates but decided to postpone it entirely.
👉 The FII is one of the Gulf's most high-profile gatherings. Over the past decade, it has become Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's premier platform for pitching his Vision 2030 economic diversification agenda to the world's most powerful financiers and executives. The postponement is a significant setback for the country's efforts to project calm and attract foreign capital at a time when [its economy is already under strain](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76203) from the conflict. 
The Houthis have continued to inflict [painful blows](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76454) on Saudi-backed forces despite months of airstrikes and a large-scale counteroffensive. On October 19, three Houthi ballistic missiles struck a military training camp in Shabwa province, killing at least 53 soldiers and wounding more than 200, according to local authorities.
👉 This is not the first time the FII has been disrupted. In 2021, most international attendees participated virtually because of COVID-related travel restrictions, with the event adopting a hybrid format. Three years earlier, in 2018, a string of high-profile executives pulled out of the summit following the killing of journalist Jamal Khashoggi by Saudi agents.
